title: Outbox and change data capture
summary: A service that changes its own database and tells other systems about it will, with two separate writes, eventually leave them out of step. This lesson states the dual write problem and its failure orders, gives the transactional outbox table and its relay options, explains log-based change data capture with PostgreSQL logical decoding and what a connector does at start and restart, the operational hazards of replication slots, how events are routed by aggregate and consumed at least once, the log as the source for derived views, a decision block over the options, and a worked sizing of an order-event pipeline.

blocks.text: The Debezium team's outbox article describes a project pattern: a public event written with the business change, captured from the log, and identified so consumers can detect duplicates after restart. Its custom transform subsequently became the shipped outbox event router. This is project guidance, not evidence that most teams copied the design.

Kafka's designers built log compaction for exactly this traffic. The design document lists database change subscription, event sourcing and journaling for high-availability as the use cases, and explains that in each one a consumer needs the real-time feed most of the time and occasionally a full load, which a compacted topic provides from the same log by keeping the last value per key.

AWS's pattern guidance recommends idempotent consumers that track processed messages, preserving the service's update ordering, emitting nothing for rolled-back transactions and using a saga when work spans service data stores. These are documented recommendations, not an account of adoption by AWS teams.

AWS's design pattern catalogue names the problem: a dual write occurs when one operation writes to two systems, a database and a message broker, and the two writes should run atomically but cannot. If the database update succeeds and the notification fails, downstream services never learn of the change and the system is inconsistent; if the notification is sent and the update fails, consumers act on something that never happened. Neither failure is exotic: a process can be killed between any two statements, and a broker call can time out after the broker has in fact accepted the message.

blocks.caption: What can go wrong when a handler commits and publishes as two steps.
rows: crash or broker error after the commit
nothing; the change is invisible downstream until a reconciliation finds it
the commit fails or the transaction rolls back
an event for a change that did not happen
two requests commit in one order and publish in the other
events out of order against the database's own history
a timeout on a call that actually succeeded
the same event twice, so the consumer must deduplicate regardless

blocks.text: Retrying does not close the gap, because the crash can fall between the two steps on every attempt, and a distributed transaction across the database and the broker is not available in most stacks and is costly where it is. The pattern's applicability statement gives the cases that need a fix: an event-driven application where a database update initiates a notification, atomicity across two services, and event sourcing, where the event store is the point-in-time record and an out-of-order event compromises it.

The principle behind every fix below is to write synchronously to exactly one system and derive the rest. The service's own database already provides atomic local transactions and an ordered commit log, so the decision is recorded once there, and publication becomes an asynchronous, retryable step driven from that record. The result is eventual consistency between services with a clear direction of flow, and no coordination across the database and the broker.

When a local database change must atomically record publication intent without a shared database/broker transaction, write its outbox event in that transaction and publish asynchronously. A request-handler broker call alone does not provide this atomicity.

subtopics.title: The transactional outbox table and its relay

blocks.text: The outbox pattern, as Debezium's blog describes it, adds a table to the service's own database. When a request arrives, the handler inserts the business rows and, as part of the same transaction, a row representing the event to be sent. Either both commit or neither does. Four of the post's table columns are shown below, and each one does a job downstream.

blocks.caption: The outbox table from the Debezium post, and why each column exists.
rows: a unique id per message, generated when the event is created; consumers use it to detect duplicates after a restart
the type of the aggregate root the event belongs to, such as Order, used to route the event to a topic
the id of the affected aggregate root, used as the message key so all events of one aggregate stay in order
the event contents: a deliberate public contract, decoupled from the internal table schema

nodes.label: Kafka topic keyed by aggregate id

blocks.legend: The outbox with a log-based relay: one transaction writes the order and its event; the connector reads the insert from the write-ahead log and the router publishes it keyed by aggregate id (s2, s3, s4).

blocks.text: A relay then moves rows to the broker, and there are two ways to build it. A polling relay queries the table for unpublished rows, publishes them and marks or deletes them; AWS's implementation has an events processing service read the outbox table and send to a queue, seeing only rows of committed transactions. It is simple, but it adds query load and latency, and rows committed out of sequence need care. A log-based relay reads the outbox inserts from the database's own transaction log through change data capture, in commit order and with low latency, with no polling queries at all. Either way, delivery is at least once: if the relay fails after publishing but before recording its progress, it publishes again, so consumers deduplicate on the event id.

The outbox is a transit buffer, not a history store, so rows are deleted once captured or dropped by partition; with a log-based relay the row can be deleted in the same transaction, since the connector reads the insert from the log rather than the table.
An outbox row that copies the internal table layout exports the schema to every consumer. The payload is a contract: version it, keep it stable, and let the internal tables change underneath.

For databases with a durable change log exposed through CDC, the log can provide a change feed without a second application write. Kleppmann distinguishes logical logs that describe query effects: inserted, updated and deleted rows, with new and sometimes old values. That turns imperative writes into facts downstream systems can consume. The exact durability, visibility and capture contract is database-specific; this is not a claim that every database implements the same logging order.

Debezium's PostgreSQL connector uses logical decoding with the pgoutput plug-in. It creates a replication slot when authorized, or uses an operator-provisioned slot. With the initial snapshot mode, it captures selected table data as well as schema information, then streams from the snapshot's consistent point. Snapshot modes, publication membership and table filters determine what is captured; configuration matters when claiming that changes are not missed. A nearly empty transit outbox cannot supply historic events in a fresh snapshot.

continues streaming from the log position stored in the Kafka offsets topic

blocks.text: Debezium runs most commonly as a Kafka Connect source connector, with change records landing in Kafka topics from which sink connectors feed search engines, warehouses and caches; it can also run as a standalone server for other brokers. Each change event carries the before and after state as replica identity allows, so a consumer can maintain any view it likes without reading the source database.

Log-based streaming avoids polling business tables for changes and can capture committed deletes. Initial snapshots, metadata queries and configured heartbeat writes still access the database. Set capture filters and replica identity deliberately for consumers that need old rows.

subtopics.title: Operating it: slots, lag, disk and schema

blocks.text: The replication slot is the part that bites in production, and PostgreSQL's own documentation says why. A slot persists independently of the connection using it and is crash-safe; it prevents removal of the write-ahead log and the catalog rows it still needs, even when no connection is using it, and that consumes storage. Its position is persisted only at checkpoints, so after a crash the slot may return to an earlier position and send recent changes again: another reason the consumer is at least once.

Slot WAL retention is unlimited by default. A configured max_slot_wal_keep_size bounds retention at checkpoint time, so it is neither an exact byte cutoff nor a precise outage timer. An unlimited setting risks filling disk; a bounded one risks losing the restart position and needing a fresh snapshot plus reconciliation. Neither guarantees recovery by itself. Measure total WAL generation and retained bytes, account for disk headroom, and rehearse recovery before changing the limit.

blocks.caption: Operational hazards of log-based capture and the control for each.
rows: WAL accumulates until the disk fills or the slot is invalidated
alert on slot lag; set the retention limit and know the resume procedure
Low-traffic captured database on a busy database instance
few logical changes may prevent timely offset confirmation while instance-wide WAL grows
heartbeat records plus a heartbeat action in the captured publication, with monitoring
a long-running read, holding locks on some engines, blocking the stream
snapshot from replicas or incrementally; Shopify's largest tables took hours
Schema change on a captured table
a registry with compatibility rules; capture an outbox rather than raw tables
idempotent consumers keyed on the event id

blocks.text: Distinguish a quiet captured table from a low-traffic database on a busy PostgreSQL instance. Instance-wide WAL can accumulate even when that database yields little logical traffic. Debezium heartbeat records help commit offsets for filtered traffic; heartbeat.action.query creates a change in the captured database when otherwise insufficient activity arrives. Its table must be included in the publication and capture filters, with write permission for the connector. Neither setting guarantees progress when the connector or broker is unavailable. Monitor acknowledged positions rather than inferring health from a configured interval.

Monitor three numbers from day one: slot lag in bytes, connector status, and end-to-end delay from commit to consumption. A connector that has been down for a day and a slot with unlimited retention is a full disk on the primary.

subtopics.title: Routing outbox events and consuming them safely

blocks.text: Debezium's outbox event router is a single message transform that turns captured outbox inserts into clean events. With its default configuration it expects the four columns above: the event id becomes a message header that consumers can use to remove duplicates; the aggregate type is appended to a topic name, so inserts with type customers and type orders are emitted to two topics; and the aggregate id becomes the message key, which the documentation calls important for maintaining correct order in Kafka partitions, since all events of one aggregate then land in one partition.

blocks.caption: What the router does with each column, from its documentation's default configuration.
rows: the suffix of the topic name
all events of one aggregate in one partition, in commit order
the public event, optionally as JSON or Avro

blocks.text: Delivery semantics require cooperation. Kafka producer idempotence and transactions can protect Kafka-side processing, but do not automatically make an arbitrary external effect atomic with offset acknowledgement. In this design, retries may redeliver events. An inbox inserted in the same local transaction as a database effect can reject duplicates; a versioned upsert may be naturally idempotent. An external API needs its own idempotency contract or reconciliation. This is a scoped failure model, not a claim that all effects outside Kafka necessarily have identical semantics.

Ordering is per key, not global. A consumer may assume that the events of one order arrive in order, because they share a partition, and must not assume anything about the order of events across different orders. Where a database offers its own change stream the same rules appear in its terms: DynamoDB Streams records item-level modifications in a time-ordered sequence kept for 24 hours, each record appears exactly once in the stream, and records for one item appear in the sequence of the item's modifications.
Key by aggregate id, deduplicate by event id in the same transaction as the effect, and rely on order only within one key.

subtopics.title: The log as the source of truth for derived data

blocks.text: Kleppmann's talk generalises the pattern beyond service integration. Replicas, secondary indexes, caches and materialized views are derived data, computed from primary data and its changes. The application that manages its own cache through read, miss, database lookup and cache write is maintaining a view by hand. The talk argues for maintaining such views from a stream of changes instead. Correctness still depends on the view function, ordering and the snapshot-and-retention contract described below; streaming is not a guarantee of bug-free results.

Kafka compaction retains at least the latest known value per key, not exactly one physical record immediately. Older records may remain until compaction, and deletion tombstones have retention constraints. A latest-state feed is useful only if some producer or materializer actually supplies complete state and deletion semantics. Partial business events do not become snapshots merely by compacting them. Otherwise rebuild from a consistent source snapshot and the retained change suffix, preserving a boundary that prevents gaps between snapshot and stream.

blocks.caption: Derived views fed from the change log, and what each needs.
rows: the after state of each change
snapshot plus retained changes, or a full-state compacted topic if explicitly built
a lag between commit and searchability
invalidation or the new value per key
stale reads within the lag; read your own writes from the primary
replay from the earliest retained offset or a snapshot
snapshot plus retained public events from a coordinated boundary

blocks.text: Every view lags its source. Read the primary for immediate read-your-own-write requirements and reconcile views that need stronger correctness. Rebuildability is conditional: the snapshot must match a known log boundary and the suffix must remain retained throughout rebuilding. If the boundary is lost, restart with a new snapshot rather than pretending partial history is complete. A view is not automatically one replay away simply because the system uses Kafka.
Define each derived view's computation and recovery contract: snapshot boundary, retained change history, deletion semantics and allowed staleness. Replay is safe only while that contract holds.

The options differ in what they guarantee, what they couple, and what they cost to operate, and the choice is per system class rather than once for an organisation. The decision block gives each option, the case it fits, the case it does not, and an example; the cites in the caption are the sources each row rests on.

blocks.caption: Mechanisms for telling other systems about a change, from a synchronous dual write to database-native streams (s1, s2, s4, s10, s12).

rows.pick_when: the consumer is non-critical, a daily reconciliation is acceptable, and the broker is unreachable from the transaction's scope
rows.avoid_when: any consumer whose correctness matters, event sourcing, or anywhere an out-of-order or missing event costs money
rows.example: a best-effort analytics ping, repaired nightly from the source

rows.option: Outbox table with a polling relay
rows.pick_when: the team wants no database-level tooling, the event rate is modest, and seconds of latency are fine
rows.avoid_when: high rates, where polling load and latency grow, or where commit-order delivery across concurrent transactions is required
rows.example: a small service emitting tens of events a second to a queue

rows.option: Outbox table with a log-based relay
rows.pick_when: events are a public contract, order per aggregate matters, and the team can operate a connector and its slot
rows.avoid_when: the database has no usable logical log, or nobody will own slot lag and disk
rows.example: an order service publishing OrderPlaced and OrderPaid keyed by order id

rows.pick_when: internal consumers such as a search index, a cache or a warehouse that want every row change, including deletes
rows.avoid_when: cross-team contracts, since the internal schema leaks to every consumer and changes under them
rows.example: feeding a search index and a reporting warehouse from the orders schema

rows.pick_when: the store offers an ordered, bounded stream and consumers can keep up within its retention
rows.avoid_when: replay beyond the retention window, or ordering across items
rows.example: DynamoDB Streams with 24 hours of retention, each record once, per-item order

blocks.text: Two of the rows combine well: an outbox captured by the log-based relay for the events other teams depend on, and raw-table capture for the team's own derived views, with the connector capturing both from one slot. Shopify's platform shows the operational shape at scale, one connector per database shard with a transform that routes every shard's events for a table into one topic, which is the kind of decision the block leaves to the operating section.

Choose outbox events for public contracts, raw capture for internal views and native streams where their retention fits. Without a shared atomic protocol, a synchronous database/broker dual write cannot guarantee their joint commit.

worked_example.title: Worked example: sizing an order-event pipeline at 2,000 orders per second

blocks.text: An order service publishes OrderPlaced and OrderPaid events through an outbox captured by a PostgreSQL connector into Kafka, with a shipping service, a search indexer and a cache invalidator consuming. The rates and sizes are assumptions chosen to make the arithmetic concrete; the settings follow the teaching, and the SQL and connector configuration after the steps encode them.

blocks.title: From order rate to slot, topic and consumer settings
items: Orders: 2,000 per second at peak (assumption), each producing 2 events over its life, so 4,000 outbox inserts per second.
Assume a 1 kB outbox payload per event: 4 MB/s of payload is only a lower bound on WAL, not total WAL generation.
At sustained peak, 345.6 million events arrive daily. Same-transaction insert and deletion is supported by the log-based pattern; this transit table is not a replay archive.
Payload alone is 14.4 GB/hour. Total WAL additionally includes business writes, indexes, full-page images and cleanup; measure it on the real workload.

For an illustrative decimal 100 GB threshold, dividing by payload alone gives 6.944 hours, not guaranteed outage tolerance. PostgreSQL enforces its configured WAL limit at checkpoints; use measured total WAL and the setting's actual units.
Configure heartbeat interval and action for a 10-second target, with the table captured and published. Verify position advancement; downtime cannot be repaired by the interval setting.
Use 24 partitions keyed by order id. Uniform traffic averages 166.667 events/s per partition; skew can make a hot partition much busier.
Shipping's 5-second commit-to-effect target is an unvalidated requirement. Shopify's different pipeline and latency statistic do not validate it.

Only shipping keeps a full-stream inbox here: 345.6 million ids daily at an assumed 36 bytes means 12.4416 GB/day, or 87.0912 GB for seven days before row/index overhead. Search uses versioned upserts; cache uses idempotent invalidation.
If all three consumers used full-stream inboxes, they would need 1.0368 billion rows and 37.3248 GB/day, or 261.2736 GB for seven days before overhead. Those are not this design's chosen inbox costs.

Rebuild search from a consistent orders snapshot with a coordinated Kafka offset boundary, then replay retained events from that boundary. Retain the uncompacted event log for seven days and finish snapshots and catch-up within that horizon; restart with a new snapshot if the boundary expires.

Capture outbox events only, not raw orders. Events include the actual row version and fields needed for projection; cache keys use immutable order id, so no before-image is required. Search rejects older versions and processes deletion events.

Shipping must never replay side effects outside its seven-day dedupe horizon: reconcile older gaps instead. Search rebuild runs separately from shipping and preserves version/deletion semantics. Monitor slot lag, broker retention and consumer progress independently.

not outage tolerance; total WAL and checkpoints govern
Mean events per partition per second
uniform distribution assumption; not a skew bound
full stream at sustained assumed peak

blocks.caption: The returned row supplies the actual version, not a hard-coded number. This minimal projection uses id, status and version; a richer search schema requires a corresponding event contract. Same-transaction deletion remains valid for this log relay, but does not provide replay history.

Minimal setup before the transaction sample. Role creation requires an appropriately privileged administrator (CREATEROLE and permission to grant REPLICATION, or a superuser); table ownership alone is insufficient. Start capture before accepting writes because deleted transit events cannot be recovered by an initial snapshot. The connector role does not own tables; publication creation is performed by the owner.
